lede: Device and app events arrive as nested payloads, but reports, joins and most tools want flat columns with clear names. Flattening is the step that turns one into the other.
objectives: Pull struct fields up into top-level columns with clear, prefixed names
Flatten every struct of a schema with a short loop over `df.schema`
Turn an array inside a payload into one row per item with `explode`
Add time columns such as the reading's day and how late it arrived

blocks.md: `sensor_readings` has one row per measurement from a small set of sensors. Two of its columns are structs: `payload` holds what the sensor measured, and `firmware` holds the software it was running. Inside `payload`, `tags` is an array of text.

blocks.title: A nested reading
blocks.note: Each reading packs five measurement fields and two firmware fields into two columns. To sort, filter or report on a temperature, it's easier as a column of its own.

blocks.md:
To flatten by hand, `select` each field you want with its path and give it a name with `alias`. Prefixing the name with the struct it came from, like `firmware_version`, keeps names unique and tells the reader where the value lived.

`"payload.*"` is a shortcut that takes every field of a struct, but it keeps the inner names as they are. That's fine for one struct, and a problem when two structs share a field name.

blocks.title: Pick fields out by path
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

flat = sensor_readings.select(
    "reading_id",
    "device_id",
    F.col("payload.temperature_c").alias("temperature_c"),
    F.col("payload.status").alias("status"),
    F.col("firmware.version").alias("firmware_version"),
)
flat.show(5)

sensor_readings.select("reading_id", "payload.*").show(3)
blocks.note: Every row is still one reading; only the shape changed. The second table shows what `"payload.*"` gives: the struct's five fields, under their own names.

blocks.md: A real payload can have dozens of fields, and new ones appear over time. Rather than typing each path, build the list of columns from the schema. `df.schema.fields` lists every column with its `dataType`; when that type is a `StructType`, its own `fields` are the ones to pull up.

blocks.title: Flatten every struct from the schema
blocks.note: Two structs became seven columns, each named after where it came from. Run it again on a payload with a new field and the new column appears without changing the code. `payload_tags` is still an array: flattening a struct doesn't touch the lists inside it.

blocks.md:
Arrays are the other half of a nested payload. `F.explode` gives one row per item and copies the rest of the row onto each one. Do it once, on purpose, and only for the array you need as rows: exploding two arrays in one table multiplies them together.

A reading whose array is empty, or missing, has no item, so `explode` gives it no rows at all.

blocks.title: One row per tag
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

tags = sensor_readings.select("reading_id", "device_id", F.explode("payload.tags").alias("tag"))
tags.show(6)
print(sensor_readings.count(), "readings,", tags.count(), "tag rows")
blocks.note: R0001 has three tags, so it becomes three rows. Every reading in this table has at least one tag, so none disappears.

blocks.md: Event payloads usually carry two times: when the thing happened and when the platform got it. Here those are `event_time` and `arrival_time`. Flat tables usually add a few columns from them: the day, and how late the event arrived. Cast both timestamps to `long` to get seconds, then subtract.

blocks.title: The day and the delay
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

late_s = F.col("arrival_time").cast("long") - F.col("event_time").cast("long")
sensor_readings.select(
    "reading_id",
    "event_time",
    F.to_date("event_time").alias("reading_date"),
    late_s.alias("late_s"),
).show()
blocks.note: Most readings arrive within a minute. R0006 was measured at 09:15 but arrived at 09:52: 2227 seconds late. The second copy of R0011 arrived six minutes after the first.

blocks.title: A field the struct doesn't have
blocks.note: The struct has `temperature_c`, not `temp`. The error lists the fields that do exist, which is often the quickest way to see a payload's real names.

blocks.md: When a whole struct is missing from a reading, every field you read from it is missing too: no error, just empty columns. That's why flat tables keep the path in the name: a missing `firmware_version` tells you the firmware block was absent, not that the version was blank.

concept.prompt: Why name a flattened column `firmware_version` rather than `version`?
choices: It keeps names unique when two structs share a field, and shows where the value came from
It makes the column a struct again
concept.why: Two structs can both have a field such as `status` or `version`. A prefix keeps the flat names unique and readable.

concept.prompt: A reading has an empty `tags` array. How many rows does `select("reading_id", F.explode("payload.tags"))` give for it?
concept.why: `explode` gives one row per item; with no items there are no rows, so the reading disappears from the result.

concept.prompt: A reading has no `firmware` struct at all. What does `F.col("firmware.version")` give for it?
concept.why: Reading a field of a missing struct gives a missing value; there's no error.

review: Flatten a struct by selecting `F.col("struct.field").alias("struct_field")` for each field you need.
`"struct.*"` takes every field under its own name; prefixes avoid clashes between structs.
Loop over `df.schema.fields` and check for `StructType` to flatten every struct without typing each path.
`F.explode` turns an array into one row per item. Rows with an empty or missing array disappear.
Add time columns while flattening: `F.to_date` for the day, and timestamps cast to `long` and subtracted for a delay in seconds.
A field read from a missing struct is missing, not an error.
